title: Biopsy proteome scoring to determine mucosal remodeling in celiac disease
projectDescription: For celiac disease (CeD) the diagnosis and response to treatment is determined by histological evaluation of gut biopsies which depend on proper biopsy orientation and has poor inter-observer reproducibility. Biopsy proteome measurement that reports on the tissue state can be obtained by mass spectrometry (MS) analysis of formalin-fixed paraffin embedded (FFPE) tissue. Here we aimed to transform biopsy proteome data into numerical scores that would give observer-independent measures of mucosal remodeling in CeD.  A pipeline was established that employs glass-mounted FFPE sections for MS-based proteome analysis. Proteome data was converted to a numerical score using two different approaches, by calculating a rank-based enrichment score and by training a machine-learning algorithm to calculate a disease-state prediction value. The scoring approaches were compared to each other and to histology using a validation cohort of 18 CeD patients comparing biopsies collected before and after treatment with gluten-free diet (GFD). Biopsies from non-CeD individuals (n = 18) served as controls.
sampleProcessingProtocol: H&E-stained tissue sections were extensively washed in xylene to dissolve and remove mounting media. Both H&E-stained and unstained tissue sections were incubated in xylene for 2 x 5 minutes followed by 1 minute incubations in 100 %, 96 % and 70 % EtOH. The slides were then rehydrated in milliQ water for 2-3 minutes and air-dried. Approximately 2 µl of 0.1 % ProteaseMAX Surfactant (Promega, Madison, WI) in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate and 10 mM DTT (HPLC-grade, Sigma) were added to each biopsy on the glass slide, and the tissue scraped off and transferred to a PCR tube (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Transfer of tissue was repeated until all visible tissue was collected, and the final buffer volume was adjusted to 25 µl. In all experiments, 3-5 biopsies within the same biopsy block were pooled, except for the single-biopsy set-up. In the latter case, 3-4 tissue sections of one single biopsy within a biopsy block were pooled together. Samples were incubated at 96 °C for 90 minutes with shaking followed by 60 minutes ultrasonication in a water bath (Branson Ultrasonics, Brookfield, CT). Proteins were alkylated in the dark with a final concentration of 10 mM iodoacetamide (Sigma) at 22 °C for 30 minutes and digested with 0.2 µg trypsin (sequencing grade, ProMega Madison, WI) at 37 °C overnight. The resulting peptides were acidified with 0.5 % formic acid (FA; final concentration) for minimum 10 minutes and centrifuged at 8500 g for 10 minutes. Approximately 20 µl of the resulting supernatants were transferred to fresh PCR tubes for desalting and clean-up prior to mass spectrometry analysis. Samples used for examining proteome score variation within technical duplicates, serial-cut sections, H&E vs unstained tissue sections and inter-biopsy variation were analysed on an Evosep One Q Exactive HF Orbitrap system. Between 2-10 µl peptide mix were loaded onto Evotips (Evosep, Odense, Denmark) following the manufacturer instructions, except that the samples were washed with 2 x 50 µl 0.1 % FA. Peptides were analyzed with an Evosep One system (Evosep, Odense, Denmark) connected to a Q Exactive HF Orbitrap mass spectrometer (ThermoElectron, Bremen, Germany) equipped with a Evosep stainless steel ion source (ID 30 µm, Evosep, Odense, Denmark). Peptides were separated by liquid chromatography (LC) using an Evosep analytical column (Dr Maisch, column length 15 cm, 150 µm inner diameter, 1.5 or 1.9µm C18 AQ beads). We used the Evosep 30 samples per day (SPD) protocol with a 44 min gradient as per manufactor’s predefined method using as solvents 0.1 % FA and 0.1 % FA in acetonitrile (ACN). The Q Exactive HF Orbitrap was operated in data-dependent mode with a full survey MS scan range of 375 to 1500 m/z at resolution 60 000. AGC target was set to 3e6 and maximum injection time to 15 ms. The top 20 most intense ions from MS1 were selected for isolation and fragmentation with a dynamic exclusion of 30 s. The MS/MS scan range was 200 to 2000 m/z at resolution 15 000, with AGC target of 1e5 and maximum injecting time 15 ms. The isolation window was 1.2 m/z, NCE set to 28, the intensity threshold 6.7e4 and the minimum AGC target 1e3.  Samples belonging to the independent validation cohort were analysed by ultra-high-performance LC (UHPLC) and trapped ion mobility spectrometry (tims) time-of-flight (TOF) mass spectrometry.  Peptides were first cleaned by solid-phase extraction using stage tips (Rappsilber, Mann, and Ishihama 2007) with three layers of C18 Empore Extraction Disks (ref). Dried peptides were dissolved in 5 µl of 0.1 % FA and applied to a nanoElute UHPLC coupled to a timsTOFfleX mass spectrometer via a CaptiveSpray ion source (Bruker Daltonics, Bremen, Germany). Between 2-5 µl peptide mix was separated with an Aurora UHPLC column (IonOptics, 25 cm column length, 75 µm inner diameter, 1.6 µm C18 beads, 120 Å pore size) using a flow rate of 0.3 µl. Solvent A (0.1 % FA) and solvent B (ACN in 0.1 % FA) were used for a gradient of 0-35 % solvent B in 60 minutes. We operated the mass spectrometer in data-dependent parallel accumulation-serial fragmentation (PASEF) mode and recorded mass spectra for MS and MS/MS scans between 100-1700 m/z. The ion mobility resolution was 0.60-1.60 V s cm−2 over a 100 ms ramp time. Ten PASEF MS/MS scans per cycle with a near 100 % duty cycle was used for data-dependent acquisition. We applied a polygon filter in the m/z and ion mobility space to exclude low m/z singly charged ions from the PASEF precursor selection, and applied an active exclusion time of 0.4 minutes to precursors that reached 20 000 intensity units. Collisional energy was ramped stepwise as a function of ion mobility.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw files were processed with MaxQuant version 2.0.3.0. Spectra were searched against the human UniProt KB database (version of January 2022) with protein FDR and protein spectrum match at 1 %. The minimum number of razor + unique peptides used for identification was one. We used trypsin as digestion enzyme with maximum two allowed missed cleavages, methionine oxidation and N-terminus acetylation as variable modifications, carbamidomethylation as a fixed modification and maximum allowed modifications per peptides was kept at the default value of five. Protein abundance was calculated by intensity-based absolute quantification (iBAQ) with a minimum number of razor peptides set to one. Processed files from MaxQuant were uploaded to the RStudio environment using R versions 4.4.3 and 4.2.2. Potential contaminants, proteins present in the reverse decoy database search, identified only by site or identified by < 1 unique peptide were removed. Proteins without an annotated gene name were removed, and proteins that were annotated to the same Uniprot gene name were given a unique gene name identifier using the DEP R package. In cases were the match-between-runs function had been enabled during iBAQ quantification, only proteins identified by MS/MS were kept.
